title: Multi-Head Attention
oneLine: Run several attention patterns in parallel, then combine them.

paras: One attention map forces every token to mix information in a single way. Real language needs several relationships at once — syntactic agreement, coreference, local phrasing. Multi-head attention splits the model width into h smaller subspaces, runs attention independently in each, and concatenates the results.
Each head is cheap (it works in d/h dimensions), and together they let the layer attend to different things in different subspaces simultaneously.
Each head projects Q, K, V into its own subspace, attends there, and the outputs are concatenated and mixed by a final projection W^O:
sections.texNote: head_i = Attention(XW_i^Q, XW_i^K, XW_i^V); the heads run fully in parallel.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def multi_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, h):
    n, d = X.shape
    dk = d // h
    outs = []
    for i in range(h):                 # each head sees a d/h slice
        sl = slice(i * dk, (i + 1) * dk)
        outs.append(attention(X @ Wq[:, sl], X @ Wk[:, sl], X @ Wv[:, sl]))
    return np.concatenate(outs, axis=-1) @ Wo
sections.caption: Heads are independent; the final W^O lets them interact.

takeaways: Multiple heads capture multiple relationships in parallel subspaces.
Splitting the width keeps the total cost the same as single-head attention.
The output projection W^O lets the heads' results recombine.
